75.t: Changes to midtown and New York work
75.s: The Piccadilly Hotel is demolished, work is scarce, and foreign pianists arrive.
75.ch: Recent years and early piano influences
75.q: : Built an important(?) hotel. A big hotel. And it's supposed to be a park or something. They're trying to beautify Broadway.

75.s: Dance theatres, movies and vaudeville flourished then; Ramirez and Dance discuss population, the decline of Harlem venues, and past competitiveness against present mediocrity.
75.ch: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
75.q: : Yeah, movies... And believe it or not, they had a lot of Colored movies. But of course, at that time we had also entertainment, we had vaudeville...

862.t: Why fewer musicians and funerals today
862.s: Henry says good musicians died, young players do not take it up, and fewer clubs and societies mean fewer funerals.
862.ch: Decline of funeral bands and societies
862.q: Well, they had. Some of them, but you see, they just died there. And then again, these young, younger fellows come on now. They don't take up. They let the old fellows come back, you understand? I guess they haven't got as many, you understand? Because they all want them. Sacriform, sacriform.…

567.t: Crossing Canal Street, no trouble uptown, and the good old music times
567.s: White says nobody gave him trouble across town, Allen remembers the Young Tuxedo, and White says the old club members have died out.
567.ch: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
567.q: Mm-mm. None. I mean mostly all of them. I'll be weep around West we go. All around West we go. I'mma tell you the truth, most all them boys know of me. Every one of them. White like black.

794.t: Decline of traditional jazz in England and closing remarks, 1968-69
794.s: Stagg laments pub jobs, club closures and bands working on the continent, notes the 1968 tours, and describes meeting people on the American trip.
794.ch: Last tours and the state of English jazz
794.q: And this is really sad for England because to us we've gone down a stage. We got to a very good period where British traditional style bands were playing concerts. And big jobs, the Royal Festival Hall, the Conway Hall, which we've already mentioned. The Royal Festival Hall has symphony concerts…

843.t: Why the music is dying out: jukeboxes and a changed city
843.s: The city is now like a graveyard compared to earlier; jukeboxes and radio replaced bands at parties and saloons.
843.q: In that respect, it is. Since the jukeboxes, I don't know what it would be, whether it's the radio or jukeboxes or phonograph records or just what exactly killed it, but, well, even Kid Thomas, who's playing across the street, other people have used the same expression, exactly the same expression,…

887.s: Cahn estimates about 15 tribes now, up from around 12, perhaps fewer than 30 in the past, with new ones forming.
887.q: I would say there are 15 because there are no doubt. I've heard of one new tribe that's coming out this year, and there's no doubt there are other new tribes. As the population moves, they will form a new tribe.

676.t: Few places for young musicians to develop
676.s: Outside New York, jazz venues have dried up, and clubs now offer only star-and-rhythm quartets.
676.q: Well unless they’re in New York City, I mean there’s just so much music in New York, and the other places it’s just dried up, although I’m told that there’s certain pockets around the country. Certainly not Los Angeles. There’s very little out there. When Leonard Feather moved out there, I think he…

536.t: The state of jazz: clubs, festivals and jazz parties
536.s: Brown compares the many New York clubs of 1945 with today's festivals and jazz parties, arguing the business just changes shape.
536.ch: Reflections on playing and jazz today
536.q: Not that particular thing, no. I mean when I first came to New York in 1945 there must have been two hundred bars or clubs with live music. Every place had a live band. They weren’t making much money but they were working. Now if you go to New York if you can find forty joints with live music…

668.t: The decline of live music and communication
668.s: Asked where communicative music is happening today, Davern says synthesizers, a lack of clubs and variety mean the end of music as he loves it.
668.q: The tragedy here I think is we are being, we are in the wrong place at the wrong time in the sense that we wouldn’t have this problem if we were born say, for myself 20 years earlier than I was born. You, a great deal more. Because we’re witnessing the end of music as we love it I think. I think…

206.t: Playing hotels in the Catskills and shrinking bands
206.s: Hotel bands lost their horns; pit bands shrank similarly.
206.q: No. Very, very little. I worked the hotels and this you didn’t know and now you will know, I worked here, because of a couple of reasons. A good friend of mine and a wonderful saxophone player, Milty Hisler was working here. And the band played a show, that’s all, except for a dance set at the end…

496.t: Wishing for an earlier era and the state of the business
496.s: Finck wishes he had worked in 1960s-70s New York and says recording sessions have declined.
496.q: Yeah. Every now and then I wish I had been maybe a generation and a half or two generations before. I think before the music business went digital and there were some players that I would have loved to have the opportunity to work with. So yeah, once in a while. I suppose everybody does. And of…

796.t: Poconos gigs and the decline of the college jazz market
796.s: Local gigs and musicians in the Poconos, the end of Burton's group around 1971 when rock took over the colleges.
796.ch: Poconos and the Phil Woods era begins
796.q: A gig? Well I wasn’t working in the Poconos really much. I would work some local gigs occasionally and they were pretty lame. But then I got in, through Bob I met musicians who had decamped to Pennsylvania. There was Jay Cameron the baritone sax player, owned a music store on Main Street in…

325.t: Why he sold the store in 1989
325.s: Long hours, family, retail stress, Tower Records and the coming of CDs led him to sell the store after seventeen years.
325.ch: Selling the store and founding Evidence
325.q: It didn’t become untenable. What had happened was I started the store in ’72 and I sold it in 1989. So that was seventeen years. I put in a lot of hours. I put in a sixteen hour day and I had two children who were, I was really starting to miss out on, you know, their childhood. And the — so that…

541.t: Why bands and gigs are harder to sustain; jazz education without audiences
541.s: Fewer weeklong club engagements make touring costly; jazz education pioneers built college programs but audiences were not built.
541.q: Part of it is there’s not enough places to play, there again. Nowadays when I look at trying to book gigs and book tours — and it’s not just me, this is from talking with other guys — there was a time where you could go out and say okay, well I’m going to play this place for a week, I know I’m here…

210.s: Jacobs and Harris debate whether festivals have replaced clubs, where unknown players get chances, and the cost of running clubs.
210.q: I’ve got to disagree with you on one thing, Jackie. You completely forgot festivals. Look how successful festivals have been.

938.t: Changes in audiences and the club scene
938.s: Why clubs declined: urban safety, concert halls and big fees.
938.q: Life has changed drastically. I mean it used to be where the urban situation was centrally located. It was easy. There were a lot of people there, there was a certain amount of security, you didn’t have to worry about being bowled over by a bunch of thugs or by some gang members. I mean there was…

161.t: Decline of live jazz in New York bars and clubs
161.s: He explains how rents, TV and changing habits killed neighborhood jazz bars and clubs.
161.q: Yeah, yeah. But you know what happened, Monk, was that around New York, a big city like this, you know rent was fairly cheap, not like today, you know. The trouble with New York today is there are too many people with too much money. And in those days rent was reasonable, a lot of little…

750.t: Changes in the club scene, downloading and cheap part-time musicians
750.s: Live-music attendance ebbs and flows; she blames downloading, computers and players who work for ten dollars.
750.q: Well in the last — I mean it ebbs and flows. There was a period of time, I guess it was in the 80s, maybe it was in the late 70s, where people just weren’t coming out to clubs. I guess they were going to the discos. Most people. Many people. But there were still people coming to the clubs. They…

547.t: DJs, audiences and a gig that was cut short
547.s: Audiences favoring DJs, and a gig with top veterans ended when a boom box replaced the band.
547.q: Yes. And people seem to respond — talking about DJs, they seem to respond more to DJs than to the band. Every year at Lehman College where I teach we play for a Christmas party, we have the full big band, and some people will dance and will look interested. As soon as we’re off the DJ will come on…

423.t: Big band versus combo drumming and the changing work scene
423.s: Tonight Show drummers needed both rock and jazz; big band drumming needs a fuller sound than combo playing, and non-adapters lost work as jazz clubs closed.
423.ch: Rock, Tonight Show and early career
423.q: They would say the same thing. Yeah, that’s a very good point. That’s right. I couldn’t call a guy who was a straight Rock player either, because his jazz stuff would be too weak. And big band jazz I think you really have to have a little more experience at than © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

1042.t: Weekly gig at Hotel Vermont and the value of real-world gigs
1042.s: Vega plays Wednesdays at Hotel Vermont for ten years; Rowe says such gigs teach musicians to observe their audience and are rarer now.
1042.q: Every Wednesday at the Hotel Vermont. We’ve been doing that for ten years except for the little hiccup with Covid, but ten years of jazz.

982.t: New York gig scene then and now
982.s: Weiss moved to New York at the end of 1981; there were many more gigs and jazz restaurants in the 80s and 90s, and live music of all kinds has declined since.
982.q: Well the very end of 1981. By January of 1982 I had an apartment and I was in. So I’m about reaching my fortieth anniversary as a New Yorker.

426.t: Decline of studio work and the New York studios
426.s: He says the studio is technically as good as ever, though there is far less recording and many studios have changed.
426.q: I would not characterize it as very active studio time. I mean the studio is up to snuff, you know technically. I think its every bit as good as it ever was. You know Don is working here…

219.t: Multiple stages in New York, jazz clubs and the lack of a leader
219.s: Wein recalls the urban festivals, observes club audiences are tourists, and says jazz needs leaders.
219.q: The multiple stage thing happened when I came to New York and started the urban festivals. That was the first time at urban festivals. We used many halls and many facilities, and that was exciting coming to New York, the midnight jam sessions at Radio City with people lined up around the corner,…

583.s: Cancelled tours and empty restaurants cost older musicians their gigs; the Foundation paid rents and sent musicians into schools.
583.q: Sure. Obviously, now... We’ll talk about it later. The life of a musician is getting harder and harder. All the smaller clubs that used to be around are having the hardest time existing. Believe it or not, 9/11 really hurt the New York music scene in ways that we don’t realize, not just the... Of…

120.t: Steady jazz jobs have vanished, unlike Condon's tourist days
120.s: He says clubs now change bands, whereas Condon's drew transients and charter buses for twelve and a half years; today maybe two steady bands exist in the US.
120.ch: Looking back and the lean years
120.q: Well, it certainly did and then they started to put in various kinds of music -- not that I have anything against that, but I always did well when I went there no matter what their policy was; even if they had far out guys or rock guys in there -- there were people that came to hear me that didn't…
